h1: The 8 Best Electric Spin Scrubbers for Tile and Grout of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaTitle: Best Tile Grout Scrubbers 2026: Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: eight cordless electric spin scrubbers for tile and grout, from a 1500RPM Qimedo to budget long-handle units, with head advice.
mainKeyword: electric spin scrubbers for tile and grout
summary: The Qimedo Q2 is the best spin scrubber for tile and grout, the only one that publishes a 1500RPM motor and a 4000mAh battery. The HOTO Wand is framed around grout detail with 12 brush heads, and the Leebein is named for floor tile with an extension handle. The four-angle Leebein, TUYU, powerful long-handle model, Dovety and the bare-bones bathroom scrubber follow.
intro: Grout is porous, and a soft brush skates over the dirt sitting inside it. The usual mistake is buying a scrubber for its motor while ignoring the head, when the stiffness and shape of the bristles decide whether anything reaches the recessed line between tiles. A fast motor with a floppy brush just polishes the tile face and leaves the stain in place.

Our editors weighed eight cordless scrubbers by their spec pages, ranking them on the Primea score, with published motor speed, battery, head set, handle reach and grout focus counting most. Prices are buckets only. Only one listing publishes both speed and battery numbers, so most comparisons rest on design cues, and we say so where it matters.

products.name: Qimedo Electric Spin Scrubber Q2, 4000mAh Battery, 1500RPM High Power
products.verdict: The only scrubber here that publishes both speed and battery numbers.
products.description:
The Q2 lists a 1500RPM high-power motor and a 4000mAh battery, the strongest stated figures in this group. It falls in the $50 to $100 range. Published speed and battery capacity let you judge power and runtime, which none of the other listings allow. High RPM helps a stiff brush break up baked-on residue instead of skating over it.

It ranks first because stubborn, baked-on grout is the hard job, and a stated speed and battery are rare in this category. The HOTO Wand costs less but publishes neither.

Buy it for heavy grout and soap scum. The caveats are the top price here and a need for a stiff grout head. Skip it if you only wipe tile occasionally.
products.idealFor: Heavy, baked-on grout and soap scum.

products.name: HOTO Wand Cordless Spin Scrubber, Electric Grout Brush, 12 Brush Heads
products.verdict: Named for grout work and packed with twelve brush heads.
products.description:
The HOTO Wand is called an electric grout brush, ships with 12 brush heads and runs cordless. It falls in the $25 to $50 range. A dozen heads means you can swap in a narrow stiff brush for grout lines and a softer one for the tile face, which is the right way to protect glaze.

It ranks second because it is the only tool here framed around grout detail work, and twelve heads give the widest range. It trails the Q2 only on stated power, since no motor speed is listed.

Buy it for detail work along grout lines. The caveats are no motor speed and a large head collection to manage. Skip it if you want published motor and battery numbers.
products.skipIf: You want published motor and battery numbers.

products.name: Leebein Electric Spin Scrubber, Cordless Powerful Scrub Brush for Cleaning Bathroom, Kitchen, Shower Tub and Floor Tile
products.verdict: Explicitly named for floor tile, with an adjustable extension handle.
products.description:
This Leebein is cordless, explicitly named for floor tile among other surfaces, and has an adjustable extension handle plus eight replaceable brush heads. It falls in the $25 to $50 range. An extension handle lets you stand while scrubbing a kitchen floor, which is where grout work becomes painful on knees.

It ranks third because the extension and floor focus suit large areas, but it is not grout-specific and lists no motor figures. Against the four-angle Leebein, it trades angle control for reach.

Buy it for large kitchen and bathroom floors. The caveats are no motor figures and a general rather than grout-specific design. Skip it if you mostly clean narrow grout lines.
products.skipIf: You mostly clean narrow grout lines.

products.name: Leebein Electric Spin Scrubber, Shower Scrubber with 4 Adjustable Angles and 8 Brush Heads, Remote Controller
products.verdict: Four angles and a remote make grout lines easier to attack.
products.description:
A scrubber with four adjustable head angles, eight brush heads and a remote controller. It falls in the $25 to $50 range. Tilting the head lets you attack a grout line from the side, which gets bristles into the recess at an angle that straight-on scrubbing misses.

It ranks fourth because the adjustable angle lets you approach grout from different directions, which helps in showers and corners, but the listing focuses on shower use and offers no motor numbers. The remote is a convenience, not a cleaning feature.

Buy it for corners and wall tile with awkward angles. The caveats are a remote that is easy to lose and a shower-focused listing. Skip it if you mostly scrub open floors.
products.idealFor: Corners and wall tile with awkward angles.

products.name: TUYU Electric Spin Scrubber, 8 Replaceable Brush Heads for Home
products.verdict: A simple cordless set with eight swappable heads.
products.description:
The TUYU is a cordless scrubber for the home with eight replaceable brush heads. It falls in the $25 to $50 range. Replaceable heads matter for grout because stiff bristles wear down quickly against abrasive residue.

It ranks fifth because it has fewer distinguishing features than the picks above, no angle control, no extension handle and no motor numbers. It is a plain tool that does what it claims.

Buy it as a simple, all-purpose cleaning tool for tile and grout. The caveats are no standout feature and no motor figures. Skip it if you want angle control or reach.
products.skipIf: You want angle control or reach.

products.name: Powerful Electric Spin Scrubber, Shower Scrubber with Long Handle
products.verdict: A long-handled scrubber that touts its motor.
products.description:
A shower scrubber with a powerful motor and a long handle that reduces manual scrubbing. It falls in the $25 to $50 range. A long handle plus a motor takes the effort out of scrubbing the lower wall and tub edge, where grout collects mildew.

It ranks sixth because the motor is named but no speed is given, so the claim is hard to compare. The Qimedo states 1500RPM, and this listing does not. The head count is also not stated.

Buy it for scrubbing without bending over. The caveats are no RPM and no head count. Skip it if you want published speed or battery figures.

products.name: Dovety Electric Spin Scrubber, Extendable Handle, 8 Brush Heads

products.description:
The Dovety has an extendable handle and eight brush heads, and sits under $25, the lowest price here. A cheap starter tool shows quickly whether a spin scrubber suits your tile before you spend more.

It ranks seventh because motor and battery details are missing, but the low price and generous head set make it a cheap place to start. Power is unproven, so expect it to struggle on baked-on grout.

Buy it for trying a spin scrubber cheaply. The caveats are no motor details and unproven power. Skip it if you face heavily stained grout.

A standalone electric scrubber with a long handle, built for bathrooms and priced under $25. Standalone means it needs no accessories, but it also means you get few extras. A long handle still helps with reach.

whatMatters.detail: A grout line needs a stiff, narrow brush, while open tile can use a wide soft one. The wrong head wastes the motor. Look for the heads described in the bullets, and favor sets that include a narrow stiff option, because a grout-capable head is what actually reaches into the recess. Soft bristles suit the tile face only.

RPM is how fast the head spins. Higher speeds lift stuck grime, but control matters too, because a fast brush with soft bristles skips over grout. Check the listing for an RPM number, such as the Qimedo's 1500RPM, and treat the absence of a figure as unknown power. Speed without control is only half the story.

Battery capacity in mAh sets runtime. A bigger number lasts through a whole bathroom, while a small one stalls partway. Look for the mAh figure, like the Qimedo's 4000mAh, and be cautious when a listing gives none, because a weak battery turns a quick job into two sessions. Charge before a big clean.

Extension handles let you stand while scrubbing floors. Short handles are better for tight spots and wall corners. Look for extendable or long handle wording, and think about where your grout is, since floor work favors reach and shower corners favor a compact tool. Pick the handle to match the room.

Angle adjustment tilts the head to hit corners and edges. It saves awkward wrist positions and helps get bristles into grout from the side. Look for a stated angle count, as on the four-angle Leebein, and consider whether you scrub walls or open floors most. Flat floors need less tilt than corners.

faq.q: Does a spin scrubber really clean grout?
faq.a: It helps, especially with a stiff grout brush. Severe staining may still need a cleaner, and the Qimedo Q2 handles the most baked-on residue. Let a cleaner sit for a few minutes first to loosen the dirt.

faq.q: What is the biggest buying mistake?
faq.a: Choosing on motor alone. The brush head decides how well it works in a grout line, so favor sets with stiff narrow heads, like the HOTO Wand's. A narrow stiff head is the single most useful accessory for tile.
Not for light cleaning, but it helps with baked-on grime. The Qimedo is the only one that lists it, so others may be slower. A lower speed is fine for light mildew and fresh stains.

Listings here mention bathroom and shower use, but check the page for waterproof ratings before wetting the motor. None states an IP rating, so wipe the motor housing dry and keep it out of the stream.

faq.q: How do I clean the brush heads?
faq.a: Rinse them after use and let them dry. Replace worn heads, especially the stiff ones on the HOTO Wand and Qimedo, where abrasive dirt wears the bristles quickly.

faq.q: Can I use these on floors?
faq.a: The Leebein floor tile model is named for it, and extendable handles on the Dovety help with reach. Open floors benefit from a long handle, which saves your knees on a large kitchen.

finalTake: Buy the Qimedo for baked-on grout and soap scum, and the HOTO Wand if you want a grout-focused set of heads for less. The Leebein models suit floors and awkward angles, and the TUYU is a plain all-rounder. Treat the cheaper unnamed scrubbers as light-duty tools. For heavy staining, pair any of these with a cleaner and a stiff head.
